name: PBT (Polybutylene Terephthalate)
chemical_makeup: Polybutylene terephthalate (CAS 24968-12-5) — a semi-crystalline polyester of terephthalic acid and 1,4-butanediol. Chemically a relative of PET/PETG, but the butanediol unit and the retained crystallinity give lower moisture uptake, better fatigue and creep resistance and a higher continuous-use temperature than the amorphous PET-family copolyesters, at the cost of crystalline shrinkage that behaves more like nylon or POM than like PETG.
summary: A niche standalone semi-crystalline polyester, distinct from the catalog's pc-pbt blend. Its selling points are impact toughness that survives the cold (IZOD 80 J/m at 23 °C, still 60 J/m at -30 °C), 170 % elongation and low moisture pickup. Its costs are a 100-130 °C bed, semi-crystalline shrinkage that makes large flats warp-prone, and very thin documentation — one dedicated filament TDS and a glass-filled Amazon SKU are essentially the whole market. Heat resistance is real but modest: Vicat 110 °C, well below the pc-pbt blend's 140 °C HDT.

printing.notes: Nozzle 235-265 °C and bed 100-130 °C are from the help3d.it PBT TDS (which also notes melt temperature can be as low as 270 °C). That bed range is the headline number: it sits above base abs's 90-110 °C and far above any PETG-family material, and it is a direct consequence of semi-crystalline shrinkage and the adhesion needed to fight it. A capable high-temperature bed and PEI sheet rated for sustained 120 °C+ service are prerequisites. Fan, enclosure and speed are not specified in the sourced TDS (unverified): the recorded fan-off setting and enclosure_recommended: true are inferred by analogy with other semi-crystalline engineering filaments (nylon, POM), where cooling splits layers and a draft-free warm chamber is what keeps large parts flat. heated_chamber_required is left false because no manufacturer specifies an actively heated chamber; treat that as untested rather than confirmed. Print speed is deliberately omitted — no figure is published. Unfilled PBT is not abrasive and runs on brass; CC3D's glass-filled 'PBT Pro' would need a hardened nozzle and is not this entry.

feeding.notes: Rigid and non-abrasive in unfilled form, so any extruder feeds it and no spool-side assistant is needed. AMS status is recorded conditional rather than yes because no vendor documents this material in a consumer material station (unverified) and the practical obstacle is thermal: a 100-130 °C bed radiates heat that most AMS units are not intended to sit beside, and the enclosure wants to stay warm and closed. Mechanically there is no known feed-path risk. CC3D's glass-filled 'PBT Pro' variant is abrasive and would wear AMS PTFE (general GF practice, not confirmed for that SKU — unverified). No Shore rating applies; this is a rigid grade.

drying.dryness_validation: No popping or crackling and no visible steam at the nozzle; consistent glossy extrusion without bubbles; no delamination or brittle snapping in a tall test coupon
drying.notes: The sourced help3d.it TDS publishes no drying schedule (unverified). Industrial PBT resin practice runs hot — commonly ~120 °C for 3-4 h — but that is a resin-dryer figure and exceeds what filament spools tolerate, so the recorded 70-90 °C / 4-6 h is the practical filament-scale adaptation rather than a manufacturer specification. PBT absorbs less water than PET-family amorphous copolyesters, so drying is a recovery step after exposure rather than routine practice.

storage.recommendations: Airtight bag or drybox with desiccant as standard polyester-filament practice, though tolerance for open-air storage is better than PETG's given PBT's lower moisture uptake

price.notes: No live retail price page was successfully confirmed in research (unverified). CC3D's glass-filled PBT Pro is listed on Amazon in the general specialty-engineering tier and Polymaker's PC-PBT showed as discontinued at one retailer. The recorded band is an estimate for niche engineering filaments of this class, not a sourced figure — treat it as indicative only.

recommended: snap-fits and connectors needing fatigue resistance
parts that must stay tough at sub-zero temperatures
components exposed to oils, fuels and solvents
parts where PETG's moisture pickup is a problem
not_recommended: large flat parts (semi-crystalline shrinkage warps them)
printers without a bed capable of a sustained 100-130 °C
projects needing colour choice or community profiles — the market is a handful of SKUs
applications needing the pc-pbt blend's 140 °C HDT

properties.notes: help3d.it PBT TDS, ASTM methods: density 1.25 g/cm³; tensile 50 MPa at yield / 46 MPa at break (D638); elongation at break 170 % (D638), notably higher than PETG, CPE or ABS and consistent with PBT's fatigue-toughness reputation; tensile modulus 2.2 GPa (D790); flexural strength 80 MPa; flexural modulus ≈2100 MPa (2.1 GPa, corrected 2026-08-01 — see below); IZOD 80 J/m at 23 °C and 60 J/m at -30 °C (D256) — the cold-temperature retention is a PBT hallmark and the main reason to choose it; Vicat softening 110 °C (Method B, 50 °C/h, 50 N). The sheet prints that flexural modulus as '2,1 MPa'; re-verification on 2026-08-01 confirmed it is a units error and it is now recorded as 2.1 GPa. A flexural modulus below the same document's own 80 MPa flexural strength is physically impossible for this polymer class, the adjacent 2.2 GPa tensile modulus fixes the decade, and FlashForge's PBT-GF TDS independently reports modulus of elasticity 3700-4000 MPa for a glass-filled PBT, placing the PBT family in the ~2000-4000 MPa band rather than at single-digit MPa. HDT is not published (unverified) and is deliberately omitted — Vicat 110 °C is the closest available proxy but is not the same measurement, so writing it into heat_deflection_c would misrepresent it. Tg is likewise omitted: general polymer literature places PBT's Tg at roughly 40-60 °C against a melting point near 220-225 °C, but no filament datasheet confirms it, and for a semi-crystalline polymer service temperature is governed by crystallinity rather than Tg the way it is for amorphous PETG or CPE. Max service temperature is unpublished; for contrast the catalog's pc-pbt blend measures HDT 107 °C @0.45 MPa with Polymaker quoting 140 °C in its own literature, meaningfully above pure PBT because the PC phase carries the heat resistance. Shrinkage is unpublished but is qualitatively the material's main handling problem.

compatibility.notes: No co-printing behaviour is documented for pure PBT in any sourced material (unverified). Self-bonding is assumed, and bonding to the pc-pbt blend is plausible because that blend contains a PBT phase — but the blend prints in a 100-110 °C chamber and neither pairing has been tested. Bonding to the amorphous polyester family (pet, petg, pctg, cpe) is chemically arguable but practically doubtful given the crystallinity difference and the 100-130 °C bed, so it is deliberately not listed. Does not bond to PLA. HIPS is the practical breakaway support at these bed temperatures, carried from the pc-pbt entry rather than documented for PBT (unverified); PVA and BVOH degrade well below the print window.

plate_recommendations.notes: Requires a sheet rated for sustained 100-130 °C service. Adhesion behaviour for PBT specifically is not documented in the available TDS (unverified) — expect to need an adhesion promoter and a brim given semi-crystalline shrinkage.
High-temperature-rated smooth PEI with an adhesion aid is the reasonable default for a warp-prone semi-crystalline material, by analogy with nylon and PC practice (unverified for PBT).
Tolerates the bed temperature; adhesion for PBT is undocumented (unverified).
Suits the high bed range; PBT-specific adhesion is undocumented (unverified).
The plate's thermal ceiling sits below this material's 100-130 °C bed range.
Polypropylene sheet is not rated for a sustained 100-130 °C bed.

alternatives.reason: The blend, and far better documented: stronger (50.4 MPa, compression 8 vs 7), much hotter (HDT ~140 °C against PBT's 110 °C Vicat, temp 8 vs 5), better dimensional stability (7 vs 5) and actually cheaper ($36-37 vs $40-70) — at the cost of a mandatory maintained 100-110 °C heated chamber and harder printing (ease 3 vs 4).

If the draw was simply a tough, water-tolerant polyester, PETG is far easier (ease 7 vs 4, warp 3 vs 7), needs no 100-130 °C bed, bonds far better (adhesion 9 vs 6) and is universally available at $18-42/kg — with lower heat and chemical tolerance and none of PBT's -30 °C impact retention.

The closest well-supported semi-crystalline polyester: slightly more heat (temp 6 vs 5), better water tolerance (9 vs 8) and a far deeper filament market at $18-35/kg against PBT's single dedicated TDS — but it warps just as much (7, equal) and lacks the cold-impact toughness.

When the cold-impact and chemical brief also needs real heat and stiffness: compression 8 vs 7 and temp 7 vs 5 with HDT@0.45 MPa 175 °C, at far lower warp (3 vs 7) — paid for with ~$65-77/kg, a hardened nozzle, a 250-300 °C nozzle window and nylon drying.

primary_emissions: terephthalate-related decomposition compounds (extrapolated from the polyester family, unverified)
emissions.notes: No emissions measurement for filament-grade PBT was found (unverified). As a polyester processed at 235-265 °C the species profile should resemble PETG's — no styrene, mild odour — but the higher processing and bed temperatures push particulate output above the PETG baseline, and a warm closed enclosure concentrates whatever is emitted until the door opens. Standard room ventilation is a reasonable precaution pending better data.

safety_notes: The 100-130 °C bed is a genuine burn hazard well beyond typical hobby printing and needs a bed and magnetic sheet rated for it — running an unrated PEI sheet at 130 °C can delaminate the coating. CC3D's glass-filled PBT variant is abrasive, requires a hardened nozzle, and its sanding dust should not be inhaled.
additional_notes: Distinct from the catalog's pc-pbt entry, which is a PC/PBT alloy in the polycarbonate family: that blend is stiffer, hotter (HDT 107 °C @0.45 MPa) and needs a 100-110 °C heated chamber, whereas pure PBT is the cheaper, tougher, more elastic and more warp-prone half of that pairing. The dedicated-filament market for pure PBT is very small — help3d.it's PBT filament and CC3D's glass-filled 'PBT Pro' were the only SKUs surfaced in research — so expect little community tuning knowledge and no vendor slicer profiles.

sources: data/filaments/pc-pbt.json (internal calibration reference, not an independent source)
provenance.conflicts: Confidence is low because a single niche filament TDS (help3d.it) supplies essentially all the mechanical and thermal data, with no second manufacturer to cross-check it. Specific gaps and flags: (1) RESOLVED 2026-08-01 — that TDS lists flexural modulus as '2,1 MPa'; re-fetching the help3d.it datasheet directly confirmed a units error rather than a downstream transcription slip, because the same document reports flexural strength 80 MPa and tensile modulus 2.2 GPa, and a modulus below the material's own strength is physically impossible for a thermoplastic of this class. FlashForge's PBT-GF TDS corroborates the band with modulus of elasticity 3700-4000 MPa (X-Y) correctly expressed in the thousands of MPa. properties.notes now records ≈2100 MPa (2.1 GPa) instead of the published figure — this is the one value in this entry deliberately departed from its source; (2) fan setting, enclosure requirement and print speed are not specified and are inferred from semi-crystalline-engineering-filament practice (nylon, POM); (3) no drying schedule is published — the recorded 70-90 °C / 4-6 h is a filament-scale adaptation of industrial ~120 °C resin-drying practice, which spools cannot survive; (4) HDT, Tg and max service temperature are all unpublished and deliberately omitted rather than proxied from the Vicat figure or from general polymer literature; (5) hygroscopy 'low' rests on general PBT polymer literature, not a filament-specific statement; (6) no co-printing, support-material or build-plate behaviour is documented for PBT at all, so the compatibility and plate sections are analogy-based; (7) no live retail price was confirmed; (8) outdoor suitability is 'limited' as a polyester-family default with no UV data published. Anyone relying on this entry for a load-bearing or thermal application should re-verify against a second source. Re-verification 2026-08-01: the help3d.it TDS was re-fetched live and every other recorded figure matched as published; only the flexural-modulus units error was corrected. Confidence stays low because the single-TDS sourcing problem behind gaps (2)-(8) is unchanged — the FlashForge PBT-GF sheet corroborates a modulus band, not this unfilled grade's other properties.
